hints: Experimental probability uses what really happened: (times it happened) ÷ (total tries). How many customers ordered strawberry, and how many customers were there?
Example: Kyle rolled a number cube 60 times and got a 6 fifteen times. P(6) = 15/60 = 1/4. Count on top, total on the bottom, then simplify.
9 of the 36 customers ordered strawberry, so P(strawberry) = 9/36. Divide top and bottom by 9: 9/36 = 1/4. The answer is B.

wrong.A: You put 1 over the 9 strawberry orders, as if you forgot to compare 9 to the whole group of customers.
wrong.C: You may have divided 36 by 12 or mixed up the numbers, so the fraction doesn't match 9 out of 36.
wrong.D: You used the customers who did not order strawberry as the top number, so you found the opposite of what was asked.

hints: First find each color's probability: marbles of that color ÷ all the marbles. Then ask: what part of the 50 draws should be that color?
Example: a spinner is 1/4 red. Spin it 40 times and you expect about 1/4 · 40 = 10 reds. Expected count = probability · number of tries.
There are 10 marbles. Red: 6/10 · 50 = 30, so 2a is YES. White: 3/10 · 50 = 15, not 10, so 2b is NO. Blue: 1/10 · 50 = 5, so 2c is YES.

why.2a: Expected = P(red) · draws. Red is 6 of the 10 marbles, so find 6/10 of 50 and compare it with 30.
why.2b: White is 3 of the 10 marbles. Find 3/10 of 50 and compare it with 10.
why.2c: Blue is 1 of the 10 marbles. Find 1/10 of 50 and compare it with 5.

hints: The pie chart is a sample of 60 people. What fraction of them chose bananas? Expect about the same fraction in a bigger group.
Example: 15 of 40 students in a pie chart chose chocolate, so P(chocolate) = 15/40 = 3/8. For 400 students, predict 3/8 · 400 = 150.
Bananas: 24 of 60 = 24/60 = 2/5. For 500 people: 2/5 · 500 = 200 people. The answer is C.

wrong.A: You gave the number of banana fans out of the 60 people, but the question asks you to predict for the bigger group of 500.
wrong.B: You scaled up by the wrong amount, like multiplying by 5, instead of finding how many groups of 60 fit into 500.
wrong.D: You multiplied the number of banana fans by 500, but you should use the fraction of people who chose bananas, not the count.

hints: List every outcome: each side of the coin with each number on the cube. Then mark the ones with tails AND a number bigger than 2.
Example: spin a 1–3 spinner and flip a coin. Outcomes: 1H, 1T, 2H, 2T, 3H, 3T (6 in all). Heads with an odd number: 1H and 3H, so 2.
There are 2 · 6 = 12 outcomes. Tails with a number greater than 2: T3, T4, T5, T6. That's 4, so the answer is B.

wrong.A: You may have only counted the number of coin sides, or just the tails choice with a number, instead of listing every tails outcome with a number greater than 2.
wrong.C: You may have counted all the outcomes with tails, or all the numbers on the cube, instead of only the numbers greater than 2.
wrong.D: You may have counted every possible outcome from the coin and the cube, not just the ones with tails and a number greater than 2.

hints: For two spins, multiply: P(first spin) · P(second spin). Write each part as a fraction out of 4 first. Watch for a number that isn't on the spinner.
Example: a spinner with 1, 2, 3, 4 is spun twice. P(3, then a number greater than 1) = 1/4 · 3/4 = 3/16. Out of 16 equally likely pairs, 3 work.
After a dog wins 1st place, can that same dog also win 2nd place? How many dogs are left to choose from for 2nd?
Example: 5 students run a race. Any of the 5 can finish 1st, then 4 are left for 2nd and 3 for 3rd: 5 · 4 · 3 = 60 ways. Each place has one fewer choice, because nobody finishes twice.
9 dogs can win 1st. That dog is out, so 8 can win 2nd. 9 · 8 = 72 ways, answer C. (81 = 9 · 9 would let the same dog win both ribbons.)

wrong.A: You added 9 + 8 instead of multiplying, so you only counted the dogs once instead of counting the ways to pair up the two ribbons.
wrong.B: You multiplied 9 · 2, thinking each dog could get either ribbon, but you forgot that the second ribbon has fewer dogs left to choose from.
wrong.D: You multiplied 9 · 9, forgetting that the dog who won the first ribbon can't also win the second ribbon.

hints: How many letters can each wheel show? Any wheel can show any letter, even one another wheel shows. How many codes are possible, and how many of them are F-F-F?
Example: a 4-digit ATM password where digits can repeat. Each digit has 10 choices: 10 · 10 · 10 · 10 = 10,000 passwords. Only one is 1234, so P(1234) = 1/10,000.
Each wheel has 6 letters (A–F): 6 · 6 · 6 = 216 codes. Only one is F-F-F, so P = 1/216. The answer is D.

wrong.A: 1/6 is the chance for just one wheel. The lock has three wheels, and all three must show F.
wrong.B: You added 6 + 6 + 6 = 18. Each new wheel multiplies the number of codes; it doesn’t add to it.
wrong.C: 6 · 6 = 36 counts only two wheels. Don’t forget the third wheel.

hints: A fair sample gives every person in the city the same chance to be picked. Which choices only reach a certain kind of person?
Example: to learn whether a city wants a dog park, calling people from a vet's client list is biased: they all have pets. Picking random names from the whole city is fair.
Skate-shop customers lean toward skaters, radio callers are volunteers, and the mayor's street is one small area. 200 residents picked at random from everyone is fair, so the answer is D.

wrong.A: You picked people at a skateboard shop, but they probably love skating, so they'd mostly say yes and wouldn't show what everyone thinks.
wrong.B: You picked people who call in, but only folks with strong opinions bother to call, so they don't stand for the whole city.
wrong.C: You picked neighbors on her street because it's easy, but a few nearby people are alike and don't show what the whole city thinks.

hints: Check each statement against the numbers. The weakest inference is the one the data does NOT support. When a choice combines two options, add them.
Example: 60 students chose tablet, 30 computer, 10 textbook. "Tablet is most popular" is strong. "Most students prefer a computer or a textbook" is weak, because 30 + 10 = 40 is less than 60.
A: the zoo's 32 is the most ✓. B: aquarium 28 > museum 20 ✓. D: 32 is less than half of 80 ✓. C: museum or aquarium = 20 + 28 = 48, which beats the zoo's 32 ✗. C is the weakest, so the answer is C.

wrong.A: You may have mixed up 'weakest' with 'strongest', or only glanced at the tallest bar instead of checking whether the graph really backs up the statement.
wrong.B: You might have misread which bar is taller, or picked a statement that sounds true instead of the one the graph supports least.
wrong.D: You may have found half of 80 wrong, or compared the zoo's votes to 80 instead of to half of the students.

hints: Mean absolute deviation (MAD) is how far the values are from the mean, on average. Both means are 15. Which set's values are spread farther from 15?
Example: 5, 6, 8, 10, 11 has mean 8. The distances from 8 are 3, 2, 0, 2, 3, which add to 10, so MAD = 10 ÷ 5 = 2. Values farther from the mean make a bigger MAD.
Set X runs from 12 to 18, close to 15. Set Y runs from 2 to 28, much farther from 15. So Set Y has the greater MAD, answer B. (Equal means don't make the MADs equal.)

wrong.A: You may have thought the closer-together numbers in this set mean more spread, so you flipped which set is more spread out.
wrong.C: You may have thought that having the same mean means the numbers are spread out the same way, but the mean only shows the center.
wrong.D: You may have thought you need every single value, but the five numbers show how far the values sit from the center.

hints: Put each person's minutes in order first. With 8 values there is no single middle value, so the median is halfway between the 4th and 5th.
Example: 60, 75, 81, 85, 86, 87 in order. The middle two are 81 and 85, so the median is (81 + 85) ÷ 2 = 83.

wrong.A: You may have thought the data looked alike, or only compared a few numbers, instead of ordering each list and finding the middle of each one.
wrong.B: You may have mixed up which student had the bigger middle number, so the difference points the wrong way.
wrong.D: You may have found the gap between the two middles by halving a number, instead of subtracting the two middle values.

hints: Probability = (ways to get what you want) ÷ (all possible outcomes). How many sections show 9, and how many sections are there?
Example: on a number cube, P(1 or 2) = 2/6 = 1/3, because 2 of the 6 numbers work.
One section out of 12 is a 9, so P(9) = 1/12.
List the numbers from 1 to 12 that are greater than 8. Careful: "greater than 8" does not include 8.
Example: on a number cube, P(greater than 4) = 2/6 = 1/3, because only 5 and 6 work.
9, 10, 11 and 12 are greater than 8. That's 4 of 12, so P = 4/12 = 1/3.
Is there any section that is NOT less than 13? What does it mean when every outcome works?
Example: on a number cube, P(less than 7) = 6/6 = 1, which means certain. P(7) = 0/6 = 0, which means impossible.
All 12 sections are less than 13, so P = 12/12 = 1. It is certain.
It's often easier to count the opposite. Which numbers ARE multiples of 4? Then P(not) = 1 − P(it is).
Example: on a number cube, P(6) = 1/6, so P(not 6) = 1 − 1/6 = 5/6. The two are complements: together they make 1.
The multiples of 4 are 4, 8 and 12: 3 of 12. P(not a multiple of 4) = 1 − 3/12 = 9/12 = 3/4.
Find the total number of bars first. Then write each flavor's probability as a fraction and simplify. Which one equals 1/3?
Example: a bag has 3 red, 4 blue and 5 green marbles, 12 in all. P(blue) = 4/12 = 1/3.
12 + 10 + 8 = 30 bars. Peanut butter: 10/30 = 1/3. (Chocolate is 12/30 = 2/5 and oatmeal is 8/30 = 4/15.) So peanut butter has the 1/3 chance.
The fraction of marked fish in her second catch should match the fraction of marked fish in the whole pond. Write those two fractions as a proportion.
Example: rangers tag 20 deer. Later they catch 300 deer and 15 are tagged. 15/300 = 20/n, so 15n = 6,000 and n = 400 deer.
Second catch: 5 marked out of 25. Whole pond: 20 marked out of n. 5/25 = 20/n, so 5n = 500 and n = 100 fish. Check: 5/25 = 1/5 and 20/100 = 1/5.
Find P(green) first. Then use it on the 64 spins: what part of them should land on green?
Example: Lou hit 12 home runs in 40 pitches, so P = 12/40 = 3/10. With 30 pitches, predict 3/10 · 30 = 9 home runs.
Each bar's height is how many plants are in that height range. Add all the bars for the total. "At least 25 inches" means the 25–29 bar and every bar above it.
Example: a histogram has bars of 2, 6, 8 and 4 (20 students). P(a student is in the last two bars) = (8 + 4)/20 = 12/20 = 3/5.
For each flavor, how many topping choices are there? Try a tree: a branch for each flavor, then split each branch by topping.
Example: 4 shirts and 3 pairs of shorts. Each shirt goes with 3 shorts: 4 · 3 = 12 outfits. The tree has 4 branches, each splitting into 3.
4 flavors · 2 toppings = 8 cups: vanilla–sprinkles, vanilla–nuts, berry–sprinkles, berry–nuts, mango–sprinkles, mango–nuts, chocolate–sprinkles, chocolate–nuts.
What is the chance of guessing one question right? Each question is separate, so multiply that chance once for each question.
Example: a test has 5 questions with 4 choices each. P(all right) = 1/4 · 1/4 · 1/4 · 1/4 · 1/4 = 1/1,024.
Each question: 1/5. Four questions: 1/5 · 1/5 · 1/5 · 1/5 = 1/625.
Find each part separately: P(heads) and P(blue). The coin doesn't change the bag, so multiply them.
Example: a bag has 3 red, 4 blue and 5 green marbles. Pick one, put it back, pick again. P(red then green) = 3/12 · 5/12 = 15/144 = 5/48.
Who did Kai ask? Would students at basketball practice feel the same about a new gym as all the students at the school?
Example: to learn whether a city wants a dog park, calling only people on a vet's list is biased: pet owners are more likely to say yes. A random sample of everyone is fair.
No. Students at basketball practice use the gym, so they are more likely to want a new one: the sample is biased. He should ask a random sample of all the students.
Turn the counts into percents so the two samples (90 and 100 students) can be compared. What is true in BOTH samples?

Example: two samples of 100: tablet 60 and 69, computer 30 and 16, textbook 10 and 15. Strong: "Most students prefer tablets" (true in both). Weak: "More students prefer textbooks than computers" (true in only one).
Sports is the most popular: 45/90 = 50% and 40/100 = 40%. Art is the least popular: about 11% and 10%. Games is second in both (about 22% and 30%).
Mean = add all the values, then divide by how many there are. Each team played 9 games.
Example: 5, 6, 8, 10, 11. The sum is 40 and there are 5 values, so the mean is 40 ÷ 5 = 8.
Hawks: 47 + 33 + 53 + 40 + 57 + 45 + 37 + 50 + 43 = 405, and 405 ÷ 9 = 45 points. Owls: the total is 432, and 432 ÷ 9 = 48 points.
Put each team's scores in order. With 9 values, the median is the 5th one.
Example: 60, 75, 81, 85, 85, 86, 87, 93, 95 is in order. The 5th value is 85, so the median is 85.
Use your medians from #15. Subtract to see how much higher the Owls' median really is.
Example: if one median is 85 and the other is 81, the first is 85 − 81 = 4 points higher.
No. The medians are 48 and 45, so the Owls' median is 48 − 45 = 3 points higher, not 4.
The five numbers are the minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum. Use your ordered lists from #15. With 9 values, leave the median out: Q1 is the median of the lowest 4, Q3 of the highest 4.
Example: 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 12. Minimum 2, median 7, Q1 = median of 2, 4, 5 = 4, Q3 = median of 8, 9, 12 = 9, maximum 12.
Interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle half of the data. Use your answers from #17.
Example: if Q1 = 4 and Q3 = 9, the IQR is 9 − 4 = 5.
Use each team's mean from #14. Find how far each score is from the mean (distances are never negative), add the distances, then divide by 9.
Example: 5, 6, 8, 10, 11 has mean 8. The distances are 3, 2, 0, 2, 3, which add to 10, so MAD = 10 ÷ 5 = 2.
Hawks (mean 45): distances 12, 8, 5, 2, 0, 2, 5, 8, 12 add to 54, so MAD = 54 ÷ 9 = 6 points. Owls (mean 48): distances 4, 2, 2, 1, 0, 1, 1, 3, 4 add to 18, so MAD = 18 ÷ 9 = 2 points.
Pick a measure of spread you found (the IQR or the MAD) and compare the two teams. A bigger number means the scores change more from game to game.
Example: "Class A's MAD is 2.6 and Class B's is 1.4, so the number of books Class A read is more spread out."
Sample: The Hawks' MAD (6) is three times the Owls' MAD (2), so the Hawks' scores vary much more from game to game. (Or compare the IQRs: 13 vs. 4.)
Find two probabilities from Ella's tables: P(fall) and P(cheese). Multiply them for "fall AND cheese". Then use that probability on all 900 students.
Example: in a sample, P(summer) = 2/5 and P(juice) = 1/4. P(both) = 2/5 · 1/4 = 2/20 = 1/10. In a school of 600, predict 1/10 · 600 = 60 students.
P(fall) = 45/150 = 3/10. P(cheese) = 50/150 = 1/3. P(fall and cheese) = 3/10 · 1/3 = 1/10. Prediction: 1/10 · 900 = 90 students.
